claims.text: The initial HEA is single-phase and compositionally uniform, with no detectable grain-boundary precipitates.
Prolonged thermal exposure within the service-temperature range causes nanoscale ordered precipitates to form at grain boundaries.
Thermal exposure promotes local elemental diffusion and segregation to grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation leads to nucleation and growth of ordered precipitates.
Ordered grain-boundary precipitates disrupt local compositional complexity.
The ordered precipitates reduce grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesive strength results in brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
Relative to the as-prepared single-phase baseline, thermally exposed material will have lower fracture toughness.
Relative to the baseline, thermally exposed material will exhibit more intergranular fracture under tensile or impact loading.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to HEAs that are single-phase at room temperature at service temperatures up to 900°C.
The proposed mechanism is not expected to apply to alloys with pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates or significant phase separation.
Segregation and precipitation kinetics may vary significantly among different HEAs.
Absence of grain-boundary precipitates after thermal exposure would falsify the proposed precipitation-mediated mechanism.
Unchanged fracture toughness and fracture mode relative to the baseline would falsify the predicted embrittlement outcome.
